The 2013 WHO guidance on Pandemic Influenza Risk Management updates and replaces the 2009 guidance. This revision incorporates lessons learned from the 2009 influenza A (H1N1) pandemic and other relevant developments. The 2009 pandemic was the first of the 21st century and the first since WHO had issued pandemic preparedness guidance. Member States’ experiences during the pandemic varied, but common challenges emerged, such as difficulty adapting national responses to a moderate event when plans were designed for a high-severity pandemic. Communication was critical, with significant strain placed on health ministries to provide clear risk assessments to decision-makers and effectively communicate with the public. The 2013 guidance emphasizes a risk-based approach to pandemic influenza management, encouraging Member States to develop flexible plans based on national risk assessments while considering global risk assessments conducted by WHO. It introduces a revised approach to global phases, which are based on virological, epidemiological, and clinical data to describe the spread of a new influenza subtype. These global phases are decoupled from country-level risk management decisions, allowing Member States to tailor their responses to their specific situations and needs. The Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework, adopted in 2011, aims to improve the sharing of influenza viruses with human pandemic potential and ensure equitable access to vaccines and medicines during pandemics. It brings together Member States, industry, stakeholders, and WHO to implement a global approach to pandemic preparedness and response. The guidance aligns with the principles of all-hazards emergency risk management for health (ERMH), aiming to strengthen capacities to manage health risks from all hazards, integrate comprehensive emergency risk management into the health sector, and promote multisectoral collaboration across government and society. It underscores the importance of timely risk assessments for evidence-based decision-making at all levels. WHO’s global leadership in pandemic influenza risk management is reflected in its role as the directing and coordinating authority for health within the United Nations system. WHO provides leadership on global health matters, shapes the health research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to Member States, and monitors health trends. The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) provide a global legal framework for preventing, controlling, or responding to public health risks that may spread internationally. The IHR also establish mechanisms for collective global action in response to serious events that endanger global public health, defined as Public Health Emergencies of International Concern (PHEIC).
